works.title: NOBODY HOME
works.subtitle: Rooms after erasure
works.logline: Families disappear from their home movies, but their effects remain: chairs rock, doors close, and birthday candles go out in empty rooms.
works.proof: Build a sixty-second study from one newly recorded room sequence: a person enters, places a cup, moves a chair, and leaves. Show an intact passage, then return to a version with the person removed while the chair movement remains. Hold the empty aftermath with room sound. End with an accessible original/derived comparison. Keep the mask and any synthesized background separate from recorded pixels, so the intervention can be inspected.
works.note: Requires an explicit person-removal and compositing adapter. Removal is an authored intervention; it does not establish that the historical room was empty.

works.title: ALMOST HUMAN
works.subtitle: Unfinished gestures
works.logline: People hesitate, adjust their clothes, check a wrist, and look away. Their small unfinished gestures become a performance no one planned together.
works.proof: Make a seventy-five-second sequence from six situated gesture excerpts. Begin with one complete collar adjustment, including the pause afterward. Let another person begin a similar movement, then preserve their different outcome. Build a brief rhythm across three further gestures before allowing one participant to stop halfway. Return to the first setting after its action has ended. Use clothing, breath, and room sounds to carry the rhythm without assigning a shared emotional state.
works.note: The comparison concerns visible actions. It must preserve source circumstances rather than infer identical motives or a universal account of humanity.

works.title: TERRA INCOGNITA
works.subtitle: Material territories
works.logline: A passage through film’s damaged edges, where scratches, light leaks, and blank intervals become terrain and the recorded world keeps surfacing.
works.proof: Build a sixty-second passage from three recorded film surfaces with different visible defects. Establish a recognizable image before following a scratch or light boundary into the next fragment. Hold one surface long enough to reveal that the apparent landscape is a material carrier. Let a recognizable scene return, then end at a blank interval with its actual recorded noise or an identified original sound composition. Keep observed damage distinct from any generated extension.
works.note: A generated transition is a separate authored layer. The material-study proof does not establish a historical relationship between otherwise unrelated fragments.

works.title: SPLIT SECOND
works.subtitle: Action and consequence
works.logline: Hands release, doors close, and feet leave the ground. Unrelated recordings converge at the instant an action becomes a consequence.
works.proof: Create a fifty-second sequence around release, using six bounded excerpts with readable beginnings and outcomes. Twice cut away immediately before a hand lets go. On the third return, allow the object’s actual consequence to arrive. Align later actions by their visible phase, then let one longer hesitation resist the pattern. End on an ordinary release after the larger consequences have changed its weight. Preserve contact sounds and disclose the montage’s separate sources.
works.note: Match action phases, not alleged identical inner decisions or historical simultaneity. The primary operator’s action grammar requires an explicit adaptation for an archival montage.

works.title: CUT TO THE CHASE
works.subtitle: A shifting pursuit
works.logline: Fleeing, chasing, training, stumbling, and stopping form a shifting pursuit across cinema, until the movement itself becomes the story.
works.proof: Build a sixty-second pursuit from eight excerpts. Establish a runner’s direction, then transfer that momentum across two clearly different settings. Interrupt the rhythm with someone waiting or recovering, retaining their local sound. Resume with an action that changes the apparent relationship between pursuing and being pursued. Finish on a person who stops while the surrounding world continues moving. Compare the cut with and without sound bridges to determine which transitions carry the pursuit.
works.note: The earlier ninety-minute proposal remains a development ambition. This first proof must establish changing relationships and rest before a feature duration is justified.

works.title: KINETIC
works.subtitle: Labor and interruption
works.logline: Work repeats across factories, workshops, and homes. Its mechanical rhythms are interrupted by maintenance, waiting, fatigue, and refusal.
works.proof: Make a ninety-second passage from three documented work processes. Establish a repeated movement in each, then briefly coordinate their rhythms through an original sound phrase. Break that coordination by preserving one complete maintenance or waiting interval at normal speed. Return to the first process after the interruption, revealing something the tighter framing initially excluded. End when one worker or mechanism stops. Keep contextual views available so the shared rhythm does not erase different conditions.
works.note: Do not compress the Qatsi trilogy into one time-lapse style or infer fatigue and refusal from appearance alone. Include those conditions only when the source supports them.

works.title: ZERO MEMORY
works.subtitle: An editor forgets
works.logline: An editor repeatedly forgets the sequence it has just made, while its archive remains available. The audience begins to remember more of the film than its maker.
works.proof: Use a fixed collection of twelve short excerpts to build a ninety-second experiment. Give the editor access to the same collection throughout, but reset its declared working history at three visible boundaries. Keep a separate audit log inaccessible to that editing state. Allow repeated selections to remain, then place an intact recurrence beside a changed one in the final passage. Sound should make returning material recognizable without pretending that the underlying model has forgotten its training.
works.note: Requires a new memory-reset policy and external audit log. Persistent archive access, model training, working history, and the spectator’s memory are different things.

works.title: HOMONYM
works.subtitle: Words change worlds
works.logline: A word passes between voices and images, changing sense at each cut until speech seems to edit the world around it.
works.proof: Construct a sixty-second relay around one word with three visually legible senses. Establish its first use in an intact spoken context, then let an action carry the next meaning before another voice names it. Make the third sense alter the sequence’s tone or stakes. Return to the opening utterance with the new associations still active. Keep original speech intelligible, and test a version without explanatory captions before adding another semantic branch.
works.note: A semantic connection needs a defensible interpretation beyond a similarity score. An assembled utterance must be presented as an authored construction, not attributed to a recorded speaker as something they actually said.

works.title: ANYBODY, ANYWHERE
works.subtitle: Lives in parallel
works.logline: Strangers in different places perform related ordinary acts. Paired images reveal both their resemblance and the circumstances that keep their lives distinct.
works.proof: Build a ninety-second comparison from three pairs of situated recordings. Start with two people preparing a place to sit, allowing a moment of recognizable alignment. Let one person finish while the other waits or changes the task. Restore a wider contextual view on each side before the next pair. Conclude with two actions whose resemblance fails at the outcome. Preserve distinct sound spaces and show recording dates or unknown-date states where relevant.
works.note: Parallel presentation does not establish simultaneous recording. The initial proof preserves different times and conditions. SCION 080 is reserved for a later shared-date edition with adequate timestamp evidence.

works.title: COLLECTIVE INVENTORIES
works.subtitle: A composite day
works.logline: A day is composed from many people’s ordinary work, with one gesture taking up where another leaves off.
works.proof: Make a two-minute composite morning from five situated participants or source records. Give each one intact practical action before connecting them through washing, carrying, preparing, or clearing away. Let a handoff between excerpts suggest continuation, then widen the frame to reveal its changed circumstances. Preserve one task that remains unfinished. End by returning to the earliest participant after their action, with a different pace and sound. Identify the assembled day as an editorial construction.
works.note: The documentary primary governs source treatment. A shared action sequence does not make the recordings one documented day or their participants interchangeable.

works.title: MNEMONIL
works.subtitle: A borrowed life
works.logline: A life story assembled from home movies begins to contradict itself: familiar rooms, gestures, and recollections belong to different people.
works.proof: Create a two-minute fictional composite from four clearly attributed source passages and original narration. Begin with an apparently coherent account of returning to a room. Introduce a second recording that resembles the room but contradicts a concrete detail. Let a later voice or image expose the difference rather than repairing it. Finish by showing how the sequence borrowed its continuity. Keep actual testimony separate from invented biography, and retain the identities of the underlying source records.
works.note: The Library of Congress setting remains an earlier fictional proposition, not a claim of institutional involvement or an established source collection.

works.title: PLANIMETRIC
works.subtitle: Held frames
works.logline: Locked-off images turn rooms and public spaces into stages where routine, background activity, and a small deviation become the event.
works.proof: Stage or select one ninety-second fixed view of a room with two practical activities at different depths. Establish their ordinary relation before a small obstruction changes one person’s route. Hold the frame while the second activity continues, letting the viewer discover the conflict through timing and sound. End on the changed arrangement without a rescuing close-up. If staged, present it as fiction; if archival, preserve the actual action and camera behavior.
works.note: Static, centered, and planimetric are separate constraints. The fixed-view proof takes precedence over supporting operators that permit camera moves.

studies.title: LATENT
studies.description: A proposed environment for following modeled relationships between source records. Navigation changes the encounter; coordinates belong to a chosen representation, not an intrinsic geography of memory.

studies.title: THE VECTOR POET
studies.description: Search proposes visual, sonic, or semantic neighbors; an editor tests whether their relation develops meaning and preserves context. Similarity scores nominate candidates rather than settle the cut.

studies.title: THE EYE-TRACE ARCHIVE
studies.description: A proposed record of screen-space anchors, motion, and paths of attention through edits. Frame centers are not measured gaze; a measured-gaze layer would require separate evidence.

studies.title: OPERATIVE CINEMA — Archival Bridges
studies.description: Develops the original proposal to bridge documentary fragments with generated passages. Keep the recorded endpoints and the synthetic interval distinguishable and inspectable; test what the bridge changes instead of treating seamlessness as historical truth.

studies.title: ANYRECORD
studies.description: A broad invitation to consider discarded film, audio, still images, and other recordings. Equal consideration does not make every record equally informative or interchangeable.

studies.title: DOUBLETAKE
studies.description: A second viewing, alternate cut, or source/derivative comparison changes the first encounter. Keep the source pool explicit so viewers can inspect what the edit contributes.

collections.title: B-ROLL OF CIVILIZATION
collections.description: The central archive-based series: unfinished gestures, routine work, rooms around an event, and material that remains when a scene is over.

collections.title: EQUIVALENTS
collections.description: A proposed collection of correspondences in form, action, and affect, with differences left available for attention rather than compressed into sameness.

collections.title: UNWITNESSED
collections.description: A proposed collection about backgrounds, recorded absence, and unattended processes. The title does not certify that nobody previously viewed a source.

collections.title: MEANWHILE
collections.description: An editorial view of what another place, person, or process is doing beyond the present frame. Parallel presentation need not mean simultaneous recording.

collections.title: COMMONTHREAD
collections.description: A proposed series preserving the original epic ambition: gather the ordinary tissue between plots—care, maintenance, waiting, and shared tasks—into sustained films whose connections retain particular lives.

collections.title: EVERDAY
collections.description: A proposed recurring or looping form organized around the ordinary day. Its intentional spelling joins daily recurrence and duration; no release schedule is implied.
